title: Exam format & how the 2025/26 papers look
body:
Course 080931 (Algebra & mathematical logic). What the recent papers show:

- **Midterm (Nov 2025)** and **prefinal (Dec 2025)**: one theory question — *"state and prove one and only one of the following theorems"* (choose 1 of 2) — plus two exercises.
- **Final (Jan 2026)**: three exercises (FOL resolution ground + unification; same claim by tableau; relations: epi-mono factorization, generated equivalence, induced order) **plus** two theorems to state and prove (soundness of propositional resolution; consistency lemma for FOL resolution).
- Theorems come from the official **list of theorems with proof** (next card). Chapter 4 (algebra) has **no** theorems on the list — algebra appears only in exercises.
- Every sheet: *theoretical justification must be provided for each answer in concise but complete form*.

**Recurring exercise patterns** (see the § cards for recipes):
1. Resolution, ground then unification, for a relation property → §2.10, §3.8.
2. Same claim by tableau / semantic tree → §2.9, §3.9.
3. "$\Gamma$ satisfiable" / "$F \not\models \varphi$" by semantical means → §3.6, §3.7.
4. Relation on $\{1,\dots,n\}$: closures, generated/induced order, Hasse, epi-mono → §1.2–§1.5, §1.7.
5. Matrix rings / groups: subring, ideal as a kernel, quotient via the first isomorphism theorem → §4.1, §4.2.

Older (2015, L. Mauri) exams also asked to formalize statements and write **SPASS** programs (§3.2, §4.1).

title: §1.1 — Elementary set theory
body:
*Exam relevance: low — background only; not on the theorem list and not asked in exercises.*

**Content:** Russell's paradox (why "every property defines a set" fails); the ZF-style axioms — **extensionality** (1.1), **empty set** (1.3), **powerset** (1.5), **separation** (1.7), **union and intersection** (1.9), **replacement** (1.11), **regularity** (1.13), **infinity** (1.15); subsets (1.4).

- **Regularity** ⇒ no set is an element of itself and there are no membership cycles $x_1 \in x_2 \in \dots \in x_n \in x_1$; it is also used to prove that Kuratowski pairs behave (§1.2).
- Successor $sx = x \cup \{x\}$ adds exactly one element (because $x \notin x$) — the basis of the natural numbers.
- **Prop. 1.17:** the powerset of a universe is a **Boolean algebra** under $\cup$, $\cap$, complement (de Morgan, distributivity, …) — the model for the Boolean structure of relations in §1.2.

title: §1.2 — Binary relations
body:
*Exam relevance: high — every relations exercise is computed with these matrices.*

**Content:** Kuratowski pair (1.18) and its characterization (1.19); cartesian product (1.20); relations $R : A \rightharpoonup B$, $R \subseteq A \times B$ (1.22); relations form a **Boolean algebra** (1.27); **composition** (1.32), identity (1.36), the **category Rel** (1.37); product vs inclusion and Boolean structure (1.39, 1.40); powers $R^n$ (1.44, 1.45); **opposite** $R^{\mathrm{op}}$ (1.46, 1.49–1.52, e.g. $(RS)^{\mathrm{op}} = S^{\mathrm{op}}R^{\mathrm{op}}$); direct images (1.54).

**Matrix calculus** (finite sets; row = source, column = target):

| Operation | Meaning | Matrix |
|---|---|---|
| composition $RS$ (first $R$, then $S$) | $x\,RS\,z \iff \exists y\,(xRy \land ySz)$ | boolean product $M(R)M(S)$ |
| opposite $R^{\mathrm{op}}$ | swap pairs | transpose $M(R)^T$ |
| $R \cap S$, $R \cup S$ | | entrywise $\wedge$, $\vee$ |
| identity $I$ | diagonal | identity matrix |

**Properties as inclusions:** reflexive $I \subseteq R$; symmetric $R^{\mathrm{op}} \subseteq R$; transitive $R^2 \subseteq R$; antisymmetric $R \cap R^{\mathrm{op}} \subseteq I$. Variants used in exercises: **circular / op-transitive** $R^2 \subseteq R^{\mathrm{op}}$ (prefinal 2025, Jan 2022).

**Kernel of a relation** $RR^{\mathrm{op}}$: $x\,RR^{\mathrm{op}}\,y \iff \exists u\,(Rxu \land Ryu)$ (common image) — symmetric but **not necessarily transitive** (Jan 2022 Q1).

title: §1.3 — Functions
body:
*Exam relevance: medium — images along functions appear in proofs (stability, extra-credit exercises).*

**Content:** a relation $f : A \rightharpoonup B$ is a **function** if every $a$ has exactly one direct image (1.57); identities and composites of functions are functions (1.62); injective / surjective / bijective and mono / epi (1.64, 1.67–1.69); images of subsets along functions (1.72, 1.73); **direct and inverse image of relations along a function** (1.74); **images adjointness** (1.75) and its corollary (1.76).

- In relation-algebra terms: $f$ is total iff $I \subseteq ff^{\mathrm{op}}$, single-valued iff $f^{\mathrm{op}}f \subseteq I$; injective iff $ff^{\mathrm{op}} = I$; surjective iff $f^{\mathrm{op}}f = I$. Matrix: exactly one 1 per row.
- **Direct image** of a relation $R$ on $A$: $f_*R = f^{\mathrm{op}}Rf$ ($b\,f_*R\,b' \iff \exists x,y:\ f(x)=b,\ xRy,\ f(y)=b'$).
- **Inverse image** of $S$ on $B$: $f^*S = fSf^{\mathrm{op}}$ ($x\,f^*S\,y \iff f(x)\,S\,f(y)$).
- **Adjointness (1.75):** $f_*R \subseteq S \iff R \subseteq f^*S$.

Used in: Jan 2022 Q4 (extra credit, $(K \cup R)^e = f^*((f_*R)^e)$).

title: §1.4 — Equivalence relations
body:
*Exam relevance: high — three List-1/List-2 theorems live here; generated equivalence is an exam exercise.*

**Content:** equivalence = reflexive, symmetric, transitive (1.77, matrix form 1.78); $P$**-closures** (1.82), unique if they exist (1.84), existence criterion (1.85); **existence of the equivalence closure** (1.86, *List 1*); **analytic construction** (1.87, *List 2*) and Cor. 1.89; computing closures on finite sets via powers (1.90); classes (1.92, 1.93); quotient and projection (1.94); **partitions** classify equivalences (1.98, 1.99); **stability under inverse images** (1.101, *List 1*); **kernel pair** $ff^{\mathrm{op}}$ (1.102); equivalences = kernel pairs of surjections (1.103).

- **Existence (1.86) idea:** apply 1.85 — the total relation $A^2$ is an equivalence and an intersection of equivalences is an equivalence, so the intersection of all equivalences containing $R$ is the smallest one.
- **Analytic construction (1.87):** reflexive closure $R \cup I$; transitive closure $\bigcup_{n\ge1}R^n$; $R^{rt} = \bigcup_{n\ge0}R^n$; **equivalence closure** $R^e = (R \cup R^{\mathrm{op}})^{rt}$. On a finite set, iterate matrix powers of the reflexive closure until they stabilize (1.90).
- **Shortcut:** the classes of the equivalence generated by $R$ are the **connected components** of the undirected graph of $R$ (Jan 2026 ex. 3: one component ⇒ total relation).
- **Stability (1.101):** if $E$ is an equivalence on $B$, then $f^*E$ is an equivalence on $A$ (reflexive: $I \subseteq ff^{\mathrm{op}} \subseteq fEf^{\mathrm{op}}$; symmetric: transpose; transitive: $fEf^{\mathrm{op}}fEf^{\mathrm{op}} \subseteq fEEf^{\mathrm{op}} \subseteq fEf^{\mathrm{op}}$ using $f^{\mathrm{op}}f \subseteq I$).

title: §1.5 — Orders
body:
*Exam relevance: high — induced order is on List 2 and in two recent exercises.*

**Content:** partial order = reflexive, transitive, antisymmetric (1.104, matrix form 1.105); $R^{\mathrm{op}}$ of an order is an order (1.115); total orders (1.116); **generated order** (1.119); morphisms of relations (1.122); **induced order** (Thm 1.123, *List 2*) and its properties (1.124); bounds, maximum, supremum (1.126–1.132).

**Recipe** — "smallest order containing $R$; if none, the induced order" (midterm 2025, Jan 2026):
1. Compute $T = R^{rt}$ (row $x$ of $M(T)$ = everything reachable from $x$, including $x$).
2. Antisymmetry test $M(T) \wedge M(T)^T \le I$. If it holds, $T$ is the smallest order containing $R$ (1.119); if not (a cycle in $R$, e.g. $5 \to 7 \to 6 \to 5$), **no order contains** $R$.
3. $E = T \cap T^{\mathrm{op}}$ is an equivalence (mutual reachability); with $p : A \to A/E$, the **induced order** is $p^{\mathrm{op}}Tp$ on $A/E$ — collapse each cycle to a point (1.123).
4. **Hasse diagram:** only covering pairs, no loops, no transitive edges. The official solutions put $x$ **below** $y$ when $x\,T\,y$; state your orientation.

**Overview vocabulary** (July 2023 asked "a brief overview of order relations"): upper/lower bounds, maximum/minimum (unique), sup/inf, maximal/minimal (not unique), total order, well order (§1.6), monotone maps, lattices (sup/inf of pairs, §4.1).

title: §1.6 — Ordinal and cardinal numbers
body:
*Exam relevance: low — only Zorn's lemma is used (inside §2.6 proofs).*

**Content:** well-ordered sets (1.136) and **induction** on them (1.137); morphisms of ordered sets (1.138); ordinals = transitive sets well ordered by $\in$ (1.139); **axiom of choice** (1.140); maximal elements (1.141), chains (1.142); **Zorn's lemma** (1.143): every inductive poset (each chain has an upper bound) has a maximal element; cardinal numbers.

- Zorn is the engine of §2.6: in a **finitary** consistency poset every element is contained in a maximal one (Prop. 2.114), which is Hintikka and hence satisfiable.
- Ordinals/cardinals index arities of operations in §2.2 and products in §4.2.

title: §1.7 — Factorization and isomorphism theorems
body:
*Exam relevance: high — two theorems on the list; epi-mono and the first isomorphism theorem are exam exercises.*

**Content:** factorizations of a function (1.144); **epi factorization lemma** (1.145, *List 2*); mono factorization (1.146); every function has an **epi-mono factorization** (1.147), essentially unique (1.149–1.151); **first isomorphism theorem** (1.152, *List 1*); second (1.153) and third (1.154) isomorphism theorems.

- **Epi factorization (1.145):** given $f : A \to B$ and an epimorphism $e : A \to C$, $f$ factors through $e$ iff $\ker(e) \subseteq \ker(f)$; then $f = em$ for a **unique** $m$ (namely $m = e^{\mathrm{op}}f$), with $\ker(m) = e_*(\ker f)$ and $\mathrm{im}(m) = \mathrm{im}(f)$.
- **First isomorphism theorem (1.152):** $f$ induces a bijection $A/\ker f \cong f(A)$; $f = p\,m$ with $p$ the projection onto $A/\ker f$ and $m$ injective.
- **Third:** for equivalences $E \subseteq F$ on $A$, $(A/E)/(F/E) \cong A/F$.

**Epi-mono recipe** (Jan 2026 ex. 3):
1. $M(ff^{\mathrm{op}}) = M(f)M(f)^T$ → classes of $\ker f$.
2. $p : A \to A/\ker f$ (one column per class).
3. $M(m) = M(p)^T M(f)$ — the injection from classes to $B$.
4. Check $f = pm$.

Algebraic versions (for $T$-models, rings, groups) are in §4.2 and used in every ring exercise ("$R/\mathfrak{a}$ is a field", "$R/\mathfrak{a} \simeq k$", Sept 2023 injective $S/\mathfrak{b} \to R/\mathfrak{a}$).

title: §1.8 — Relations via functions
body:
*Exam relevance: low — background for chapters 2–3.*

**Content:** indexed families, **products**, **sums** (disjoint unions) and **powers** $B^A$ (1.156, 1.157); **characteristic functions** (1.160); the natural bijection $\mathrm{Sub}(A) \cong \Omega^A$ with $\Omega = \{0,1\}$ (1.161), under which inclusion becomes the pointwise order (1.162) and the Boolean structure becomes pointwise $\wedge,\vee,\lnot$ (1.163); relations as functions $A \times B \to \Omega$.

- This is the bridge to semantics: truth values live in $\Omega$, relations of a first order structure are characteristic functions (§3.1), and quantifiers become sup/inf over $\Omega$ (§3.5).

title: §2.1 — Overview
body:
*Exam relevance: low — orientation only, but the sound/complete picture is what the theory questions are about.*

Propositional logic has two constituents:
- **Syntax** — formulas built from an alphabet; correctness of reasoning is examined with **calculi** (tableaux §2.9, resolution §2.10, Hilbert §2.11, sequents §2.12) whose rules look only at the form of formulas.
- **Semantics** — meaning via truth values (§2.4–§2.7): when a formula is true, when a reasoning is correct.

The two are tied together by **soundness and completeness theorems**: examining a reasoning syntactically ($\vdash$) or semantically ($\models$) gives the same result. The chapter's spine: consistency posets (§2.6) → regular inferences (§2.8) → every regular calculus is complete.

title: §2.2 — Algebraic signatures and their structures
body:
*Exam relevance: low–medium — machinery behind §2.3–§2.4 and §4.2; congruences reappear in algebra exercises.*

**Content:** operations of arity $\kappa$ (2.1); algebraic structures (2.3) and derived operations (2.5); **algebraic signatures** (2.7) and $S$-structures (2.8); $S$**-morphisms** (2.10, 2.12), isomorphisms = bijective morphisms (2.13); **free** $S$**-structures** (2.14–2.16); **terms** (2.17–2.21) and the **term algebra**, which is free on the variables (2.23); **induction** (2.24) and **recursion** (2.29, 2.32) on terms; **substitutions** (2.36, 2.37); **congruences** (2.39) and quotient structures (2.41).

- Free structure = any map from the variables extends **uniquely** to a morphism — this is what makes valuations (§2.4) and substitutions well defined.
- **Congruence:** an equivalence compatible with every operation; then $M/\!\sim$ inherits the structure and the projection is a morphism. Reused for $T$-models in §4.2 (Sept 2023 ex. 3).

title: §2.3 — Propositional languages
body:
*Exam relevance: low — justifies induction on formulas.*

**Content:** connectives as an algebraic signature induced by the structure of $\Omega$ (2.43); propositional alphabets (2.44); the propositional language $L$ = free algebra of formulas over the variables (2.45); **structural induction** (2.48) and **recursion** (2.49, 2.51) on formulas; substitution of formulas for variables (2.53).

- Proofs "by structural induction on $\varphi$" (Hintikka, substitution lemma) are justified here: check variables/constants, then show the property is preserved by each connective.

title: §2.4 — Semantics
body:
*Exam relevance: low — background for §2.5–§2.7.*

**Content:** a **valuation** is a morphism $v : L \to \Omega$ of the connective signature (2.55); every assignment $v_0$ of truth values to the variables extends **uniquely** to a valuation (2.56, freeness); **truth tables** with variables $X$ (2.58), their algebra (2.60), and the truth function of a formula (2.61, 2.62).

- Practical meaning: to evaluate a formula, assign values to its variables and compute bottom-up; formulas with the same variables are compared through their truth tables.

title: §2.5 — Semantical equivalence
body:
*Exam relevance: medium — uniform notation and the substitution lemma are used in every calculus and in the theory proofs.*

**Content:** equivalent formulas (2.64), **valid** formulas $\models \varphi$ (2.66); internalization $\varphi \equiv \psi \iff \models \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi$ (2.68); equivalence is a congruence (2.69); **substitution lemma** (2.73); the Lindenbaum algebra is Boolean (2.74); **uniform notation** (2.75–2.79: α/β formulas, induction and recursion for uniform notation); definability of connectives (2.82–2.85); literals and **CNF** (2.86–2.89).

**Uniform notation (α conjunctive, β disjunctive):**

| Type | Formula | Components |
|---|---|---|
| α | $\varphi \land \psi$ / $\lnot(\varphi \lor \psi)$ / $\lnot(\varphi \to \psi)$ | $\varphi,\psi$ / $\lnot\varphi,\lnot\psi$ / $\varphi,\lnot\psi$ |
| α | $\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi$ | $\varphi \to \psi,\ \psi \to \varphi$ |
| β | $\varphi \lor \psi$ / $\lnot(\varphi \land \psi)$ / $\varphi \to \psi$ | $\varphi,\psi$ / $\lnot\varphi,\lnot\psi$ / $\lnot\varphi,\psi$ |

$\alpha \equiv \alpha_1 \land \alpha_2$, $\beta \equiv \beta_1 \lor \beta_2$ (2.76). **Induction for uniform notation (2.77)** is the induction used in Hintikka's lemma: atoms and negated atoms, $\lnot\lnot$, α, β.

- The **substitution lemma (2.73)** — replacing a subformula by an equivalent one gives an equivalent formula — is the key step in the **soundness of resolution** proof (§2.10).

title: §2.6 — Satisfiability
body:
*Exam relevance: very high — four theorems on the list; two already asked.*

**Content:** truth of a formula on a valuation (2.94); satisfiable sets (2.96); **saturated** sets = sets of formulas true on a valuation (2.103–2.105); **consistency posets** (2.106); **Hintikka sets** (2.109); **Hintikka's lemma** (2.110, *List 1*); **maximal elements are Hintikka** (2.111, *List 1*); finitary posets (2.112); **contained in a finitary one** (2.113, *List 2*); maximal extension in finitary posets via Zorn (2.114); every element of a consistency poset is satisfiable (2.115); **compactness** (2.116, *List 2*).

**Consistency poset** $C$: for every $S \in C$ — (1) not both $x, \lnot x$; (2) $\bot,\lnot\top \notin S$; (3) $\lnot\lnot\varphi \in S \Rightarrow S \cup \{\varphi\} \in C$; (4) $\alpha \in S \Rightarrow S \cup \{\alpha_1,\alpha_2\} \in C$; (5) $\beta \in S \Rightarrow S \cup \{\beta_i\} \in C$ for some $i$. **Hintikka set:** the same with "$\dots \in H$".

**Proof skeletons:**
- *Hintikka (2.110):* $a(x) = 1 \iff x \in H$; show $P = \{\varphi : \varphi \in H \Rightarrow a(\varphi) = 1\}$ is all of $L$ by induction for uniform notation.
- *Maximal ⇒ Hintikka (2.111):* each condition "$S \cup \{\dots\} \in C$" plus maximality gives "$\dots \in S$".
- *Compactness (2.116):* $C$ = sets all of whose finite subsets are satisfiable is a consistency poset; check (1)–(5), the β case by contradiction with $T_1 \cup T_2$.

Asked: compactness (midterm 2025), maximal ⇒ Hintikka (July 2023).

title: §2.7 — Semantical consequence
body:
*Exam relevance: medium — used implicitly in every proof by resolution or tableaux.*

**Content:** $\varphi$ is a **consequence** of $F$ ($F \models \varphi$) if every model of $F$ satisfies $\varphi$ (2.117); $F \models \varphi \iff F \cup \{\lnot\varphi\}$ **is unsatisfiable** (2.120); consequence rules for α/β formulas (2.123); **deduction theorem**, semantical version: $F \cup \{\varphi\} \models \psi \iff F \models \varphi \to \psi$ (2.124); internalization of consequence for finite $F$ (2.127).

- 2.120 is why every calculus works **by refutation**: add $\lnot\varphi$ and look for a closed expansion / closed tableau / empty clause.

title: §2.8 — Inference relations
body:
*Exam relevance: high — the completeness strategy for every calculus; one List-2 theorem.*

**Content:** **finitary inference relation** (2.128): identity, composition (cut), finiteness, consistency $F \vdash \varphi \iff F,\lnot\varphi \vdash \bot$; **sound / complete** (2.130); weakening (2.131); composition variants (2.132); consistent sets (2.134); **completely regular** inference (2.139), complete consistent sets (2.141, 2.142), **Lindenbaum** (2.143), completely regular ⇒ complete (2.147); **regular** inference (2.148, simplified form 2.149); **consistent sets of a regular inference form a consistency poset** (2.150, *List 2*); regular ⇒ complete (2.151); closure operations (2.152–2.154).

**Regular (2.148/2.149):** $\alpha \vdash \alpha_i$; $\beta,\lnot\beta_1,\lnot\beta_2 \vdash \bot$; $\vdash \top$.

**Proof idea of 2.150:** check the consistency-poset conditions for $C = \{F : F \nvdash \bot\}$; e.g. if $x, \lnot x \in F$ then $F \vdash \bot$; if $F \cup \{\alpha_1,\alpha_2\} \vdash \bot$ then $F \vdash \bot$ by $\alpha \vdash \alpha_i$ and cut; β case uses $\beta,\lnot\beta_1,\lnot\beta_2 \vdash \bot$. Then every consistent set is satisfiable (§2.6), which is **completeness** (2.151).

This is the template for proving each calculus complete: show it is regular (tableaux 2.168, resolution 2.184, Hilbert 2.201, sequents 2.209). Asked: "regularity of the resolution inference" (July 2023).

title: §2.9 — The tableaux calculus
body:
*Exam relevance: high — tableau exercises appear on almost every recent paper (prop here, FOL in §3.9).*

**Content:** expansion rules (2.155); tableau expansions (2.156); complete branches (2.159); **closed** branches — contain $\bot$ or a pair $\varphi, \lnot\varphi$ (2.160); satisfiable branches (2.162); expansion rules preserve satisfiability (2.164); the tableau inference (2.165, 2.167); it is a finitary **regular** inference (2.168); **sound and complete** (2.169).

**How to write one:**
- Start with $F \cup \{\lnot\varphi\}$; α adds both components to the branch; β **splits** the branch; $\lnot\lnot\varphi$ adds $\varphi$.
- Do all non-branching steps on the trunk first, branch as late as possible; mark closed branches ×.
- All branches closed ⇒ $F \vdash \varphi$. An open complete branch gives a satisfying valuation (a countermodel).

Example (midterm 2025): $x \to y \lor z,\ y \leftrightarrow z \vdash x \to y \land z$ — trunk $x$, $\lnot(y \land z)$; split on $\lnot x \mid y \lor z$, then $\lnot y \mid \lnot z$, then use $y \leftrightarrow z$.

title: §2.10 — Resolution
body:
*Exam relevance: very high — soundness asked twice; resolution exercises on every paper.*

**Content:** inference rules on **generalized clauses** (2.172): falsehood, double negation, α-expansion, β-expansion, **resolution**, cut; expansions (2.173); the induced inference (2.175); **soundness** (2.178, *List 1*); variants $\varphi \ast \psi$ (2.180) and **expansion of variants** (2.181, *List 2*); closed expansion $\iff F \vdash \bot$ (2.182); **finitary** inference (2.183, *List 1*); **regular** (2.184); **complete** (2.185).

**Rules:** α-expansion splits a clause into **two clauses** ($\{\dots,\alpha\} \to \{\dots,\alpha_1\}, \{\dots,\alpha_2\}$); β-expansion replaces $\beta$ by $\beta_1,\beta_2$ **in the same clause**; resolution: from $\{\psi\} \cup X$ and $\{\lnot\psi\} \cup Y$ derive $X \cup Y$.

**Soundness (2.178) skeleton:** each rule preserves satisfaction, via the substitution lemma (falsehood: $\varphi_i[\varnothing/\bot] \equiv \varphi_i$; α: $\varphi_i[\alpha_1/\alpha] \land \varphi_i[\alpha_2/\alpha] \equiv \varphi_i$; β: $\varphi_i[\beta_1,\beta_2/\beta] \equiv \varphi_i$; resolution: case on $a \models \psi$). A closed expansion contains $\varnothing$, which is unsatisfiable, so $F \vdash \varphi \Rightarrow F \cup \{\lnot\varphi\}$ unsatisfiable $\Rightarrow F \models \varphi$.

**Regularity (2.184):** $\{\alpha\},\{\lnot\alpha_i\} \to \{\alpha_i\} \to \varnothing$; $\{\beta\},\{\lnot\beta_1\},\{\lnot\beta_2\} \to \{\beta_1,\beta_2\} \to \{\beta_2\} \to \varnothing$; $\{\lnot\top\}$ closes by falsehood.

**Exam table format:** *Step | Clause | Rule*, reasons like "1, β-expansion", "5, 10, resolution".

title: §2.11 — The Hilbert calculus
body:
*Exam relevance: low — not on the theorem list and not asked in the available papers.*

**Content:** axioms (2.186) — all formulas of types such as $\bot \to \varphi$, $\top$, $\alpha \to \alpha_i$, $\alpha_1 \to (\alpha_2 \to \alpha)$, … (uniform-notation schemes); the only primitive rule is **modus ponens** (2.187); derivations (2.188); **soundness** (2.191); derived rules (2.192–2.196); **deduction theorem** $F,\varphi \vdash \psi \iff F \vdash \varphi \to \psi$ (2.198); finitary (2.200), **regular** (2.201), hence **complete** (2.202).

title: §2.12 — The sequent calculus
body:
*Exam relevance: low — not on the theorem list and not asked in the available papers.*

**Content:** sequents $\Sigma \rhd \Sigma'$ with axiom schemes $\Sigma,\varphi \rhd \varphi,\Sigma'$, $\ \Sigma,\bot \rhd \Sigma'$, $\ \Sigma \rhd \top,\Sigma'$ and logical + structural rules (2.203); derivations (2.204); **logical rules are invertible** (2.206); the induced inference relation (2.207, 2.208); the sequent calculus is **regular** (2.209), hence complete.

title: §3.1 — First order signatures and structures
body:
*Exam relevance: low–medium — vocabulary for writing models.*

**Content:** relations of arity $\kappa$ on a set (3.1) and characteristic functions (3.2, 3.3); **first order structures** $(M, F^M, R^M)$ (3.4); **signatures** $S = (F^S, R^S)$ (3.6, 3.7); $S$-structures (3.10); $S$-morphisms (3.12) and their category (3.13).

- An $L$-structure for the exercises = a domain $M$ plus an interpretation $[\![f]\!]$ of each function symbol and $[\![R]\!] \subseteq M^n$ of each relation symbol. Countermodels are written exactly this way: $M = \{a,b\}$, $[\![R]\!] = \{a\}$, …

title: §3.2 — First order languages
body:
*Exam relevance: medium — formalization questions (mostly older papers).*

**Content:** first order alphabets (3.15); **terms** = free algebra over the variables (3.16) with induction/recursion (3.17–3.19); atomic formulas (3.20); the signature of formulas (3.21) and the **first order language** (3.22) with induction/recursion (3.23–3.26).

**Formalization exercises** (older exams; Jan 2022 Q1): extend the language with symbols for the named objects ($h$, $g$, $a$, …) and write *(theory axioms) ∧ (hypotheses) → (conclusion)*.
- Composition of relations needs an explicit middle variable: $x\,RR^{\mathrm{op}}\,y \iff \exists u(Rxu \land Ryu)$.
- Keep existential objects (max, min, witnesses) in the same quantifier scope as the formulas that use them.
- Sanity-check the claim first — Feb 23 2015's "$x \mapsto a \wedge x$ is a lattice morphism" is false without distributivity.

title: §3.3 — Set theoretical semantics
body:
*Exam relevance: medium — the definitions behind every semantic proof.*

**Content:** operations of arity $X$ on $M$ (3.28, 3.29); every **assignment** $a \in M^X$ extends uniquely to the interpretation of terms (3.30); the **support** (variables) of a term and dependence only on it (3.33, 3.34); relations of arity $X$ (3.35); interpretation of atomic formulas (3.36) extended to all formulas (3.37); **free variables** (3.39) and dependence of truth only on them (3.40); **quantifiers as adjoints** to substitution, $\exists_f \dashv [f] \dashv \forall_f$ (3.41).

- Concretely: $M, a \models \forall x\varphi$ iff $M, a[m/x] \models \varphi$ for **every** $m \in M$; $\exists$: for **some** $m$. Sentences don't depend on $a$.

title: §3.4 — Substitution
body:
*Exam relevance: low–medium — needed for correct unification and prenex forms.*

**Content:** term substitutions as endomorphisms of the term algebra (3.42) and their action on atomic formulas (3.44); bound and free occurrences (3.46); **α-equivalence** (renaming bound variables) as a congruence (3.48) and regular representatives (3.49); interpretation respects it (3.51); substitution on formulas avoiding capture (3.52–3.54); composition of substitutions (3.56).

- In practice: before substituting $t$ for $x$ in $\varphi$, rename bound variables of $\varphi$ that occur in $t$. In resolution, **rename variables apart** in the two clauses before unifying.

title: §3.5 — Equivalence
body:
*Exam relevance: medium–high — one List-1 theorem; prenex forms in every unification exercise.*

**Content:** lemmas on sup/inf in $\Omega$ (3.58–3.62); equivalence of formulas (3.63); **commutativity of quantifiers** (3.64, *List 1*); quantifier equivalences (3.66, 3.68); **prenex form** (3.69–3.71); **uniform notation** for quantifiers (3.73–3.76).

- **3.64:** $\forall x\forall y\varphi \equiv \forall y\forall x\varphi$ and $\exists x\exists y\varphi \equiv \exists y\exists x\varphi$ — proof: $\inf_m\inf_n = \inf_n\inf_m$ (sup likewise) in $\Omega$ (lemma 3.58). Mixed quantifiers do **not** commute: $\exists x\forall y \models \forall y\exists x$ only.
- **Prenex rules:** $\lnot\forall x\varphi \equiv \exists x\lnot\varphi$, $\lnot\exists x\varphi \equiv \forall x\lnot\varphi$; $(Qx\varphi) \land \psi \equiv Qx(\varphi \land \psi)$ if $x$ not free in $\psi$ (same for $\lor$); in an implication's **antecedent** quantifiers flip.

| Type | Formula | Instance |
|---|---|---|
| γ (universal) | $\forall x\varphi$, $\lnot\exists x\varphi$ | $\varphi[t/x]$, $\lnot\varphi[t/x]$ — any closed term $t$ |
| δ (existential) | $\exists x\varphi$, $\lnot\forall x\varphi$ | $\varphi[p/x]$, $\lnot\varphi[p/x]$ — a **new** parameter $p$ |

title: §3.6 — Satisfiability
body:
*Exam relevance: very high — five List theorems; prefinal 2025 asked 3.81/3.101; satisfiability exercises.*

**Content:** truth in a structure (3.78); **evaluation and substitution** (3.81, *List 2*); sentences (3.82, 3.83); satisfiable sets (3.85); **satisfiability lemma** (3.86, *List 2*); expansions of signatures/structures (3.87, 3.88); universal formulas (3.90); **Skolemization** (3.91) and its **equisatisfiability** (3.94, *List 1*); **Herbrand structures** (3.95–3.99); FOL **Hintikka sets** (3.100) and **Hintikka's lemma** (3.101, *List 1*); parameters (3.102, 3.103); FOL **consistency posets** (3.104–3.108); every element of a consistency poset is satisfiable in a Herbrand structure (3.109).

- **3.81:** $[\![s[t/x]]\!](a) = [\![s]\!](a[t/x])$ and $[\![\varphi[t/x]]\!](a) = [\![\varphi]\!](a[t/x])$ — induction on terms, then formulas (equality, relations, connectives).
- **3.86:** if $S \cup \{\gamma\}$ is satisfiable so is $S \cup \{\gamma,\gamma(t)\}$; if $S \cup \{\delta\}$ is satisfiable so is $S \cup \{\delta,\delta(c)\}$ for a fresh constant $c$ (expand the model interpreting $c$ as a witness).
- **3.101 (Hintikka):** Herbrand structure on closed terms, $[\![R]\!]$ = atoms in $H$; induction for uniform notation; γ/δ cases use that every element is a closed term (3.99).
- **FOL consistency poset:** the 5 propositional conditions plus γ: $S \cup \{\gamma(t)\} \in C$ for every closed $t$; δ: $S \cup \{\delta(p)\} \in C$ for some new $p$.

**"**$\Gamma$ **is satisfiable" exercises:** give one explicit finite structure and check every formula with its witnesses. Classic answers: 3-cycle $0\to1\to2\to0$; path $0 - 1 - 2$ (reflexive symmetric); a hub element related to/from everything.

title: §3.7 — Semantical consequence
body:
*Exam relevance: medium — entailment/non-entailment exercises.*

**Content:** $\Gamma \models \varphi$ (3.111); **deduction theorem** (3.112); $\Gamma \models \varphi \iff \Gamma \cup \{\lnot\varphi\}$ **is unsatisfiable** (3.113); weakening (3.114); 3.115; closure of a set of sentences (3.116), **theories** and axiomatizations (3.117), models of a set of sentences (3.118).

| Asked | Show |
|---|---|
| $F \models \varphi$ | every $M \models F$ satisfies $\varphi$ (argue generally, Feb 2015 Q2) |
| $F \not\models \varphi$ | one $M \models F$ with $M \not\models \varphi$ |
| $\varphi$ not valid | one $M \not\models \varphi$ |

Sept 2023 ex. 2: $\forall x(Rx \to Sx),\ \exists x(Sx \to Tx) \not\models \forall x(Rx \to Tx)$ — an open leaf of a semantic tree gives $M = \{a,b\}$, $[\![R]\!] = \{a\}$, $[\![S]\!] = \{a,b\}$, $[\![T]\!] = \{b\}$.

title: §3.8 — Resolution
body:
*Exam relevance: very high — the most frequent exercise type, plus a List-2 theorem asked in Jan 2026.*

**Content:** **soundness** (3.121); **consistency lemma for resolution** (3.122, *List 2*); **completeness** (3.123); unifiable sets of literals (3.124); **Robinson's unification algorithm** (3.125); **Skolem normal form** (3.129); **resolution with unification** (3.130): resolvent $[(C_1 \setminus E_1) \cup (C_2 \setminus E_2)]u$ with $u$ an mgu of $\bar E_1 \cup E_2$ (factoring built in; rename clauses apart first).

**Ground (Herbrand-style) recipe:** assumptions = premises + negated goal; δ-expand the negated goal and the existentials (new parameters); γ-instantiate the axioms exactly on the parameters your diagram needs; β-expand implications into clauses; resolve.

**Unification pipeline** (table *Formula | Prenex | Skolemization | Clausal form*): negate goal → prenex → Skolemize ($\exists y$ ↦ function of the universals to its left, constant if none) → clauses → resolve starting from the negated-goal unit clause (SLD works: these are Horn).

**Consistency lemma (3.122) skeleton:** $C$ = finite sets with no closed expansion; check each condition by contradiction, composing expansions ($S \mapsto \alpha_1,\alpha_2$ then $S \cup \{\alpha_1,\alpha_2\} \mapsto \bot$ gives $S \mapsto \bot$; β via variants; δ with a fresh parameter).

Asked: consistency lemma (Jan 2026); resolution exercises on every paper (serial+symmetric+transitive ⇒ reflexive; reflexive+circular ⇒ symmetric; composition of "surjective" relations).

title: §3.9 — Tableaux
body:
*Exam relevance: high — tableau/semantic-tree exercises are on almost every paper.*

**Content:** FOL tableau rules (3.133): **γ** — add $\gamma(t)$ for any closed term $t$; **δ** — add $\delta(p)$ for a parameter $p$ **not yet on the branch**; $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ if some finite $\Gamma' \cup \{\lnot\varphi\}$ has a closed tableau; **soundness** (3.135); sets without closed tableau form a consistency poset (3.138); **completeness** (3.139).

**Tips:** δ before γ (introduce witnesses, then instantiate universals on them); γ can be reused; δ on an existential **premise** also needs a fresh constant.

**Semantic trees:** nodes are sets of formulas; expand one formula per step (same α/β/γ/δ). All leaves unsatisfiable ⇒ the root set is unsatisfiable ($\vdash$ proved); an open saturated leaf ⇒ satisfiable, and its literals **are** a countermodel.

Asked: Jan 2026 ex. 2 (tableau), prefinal 2025 ex. 3 (tableau + semantic tree), Sept 2023 ex. 2 (semantic tree, non-entailment).

title: §3.10 — The Hilbert calculus
body:
*Exam relevance: low — not on the theorem list and not asked in the available papers.*

**Content:** axiom schemes (3.140): $\varphi \to (\chi \to \varphi)$; $(\varphi \to (\chi \to \psi)) \to ((\varphi \to \chi) \to (\varphi \to \psi))$; $\bot \to \varphi$; $\varphi \to \top$; $\lnot\lnot\varphi \to \varphi$; $\varphi \to (\lnot\varphi \to \chi)$; $\alpha \to \alpha_i$; $(\beta_1 \to \varphi) \to ((\beta_2 \to \varphi) \to (\beta \to \varphi))$; $\gamma \to \gamma(t)$. Rules: **modus ponens** and **generalization**. Deduction theorem (3.142), soundness (3.144), completeness (3.147).

title: §4.1 — Algebraic theories and their models
body:
*Exam relevance: high — groups/rings/lattices are the algebra exercises; no theorems on the list.*

**Content:** algebraic signatures (only function symbols, 4.1); **algebraic theories** — axiomatized by quantifier-free atomic formulas, i.e. equations $s = t$ (4.2); $T$-algebras and morphisms form a category (4.3, 4.4); **groups** (4.5, 4.6) — a function is a group morphism **iff it preserves the product** (4.8); **rings** (4.10, 4.11) and ring morphisms (4.14); vector spaces (4.15–4.19); $k$-algebras (4.21); **lattices** (4.23); Boolean algebras (4.24).

- **Prop. 4.8** is exactly Feb 2 2015 Q1 ("if $h$ preserves the product, then $h$ is a morphism of groups"): $h(1) = h(1\cdot1) = h(1)h(1) \Rightarrow h(1) = 1$; $h(x)h(x^{-1}) = h(1) = 1 \Rightarrow h(x^{-1}) = h(x)^{-1}$.
- Axioms to write when formalizing: groups (associativity, $x1 = 1x = x$, $xx^{-1} = x^{-1}x = 1$); lattices (associativity, commutativity of $\wedge,\vee$, absorption), order $x \le y \iff x \wedge y = x$.
- **SPASS** (older exams): DFG format `begin_problem` … `list_of_symbols` (`functions[(mul,2),(inv,1),(one,0)]`) … `list_of_formulae(axioms)` / `list_of_formulae(conjectures)` with `formula(forall([x,y],equal(…,…)))` … `end_problem.`

**Matrix-ring trick:** write elements as polynomials in a special matrix — $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&a\end{pmatrix} = aI+bN$ ($N^2=0$, $\cong \mathbf{R}[x]/(x^2)$); $\begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\0&a&b\\0&0&a\end{pmatrix} = aI+bN+cN^2$ ($N^3=0$); $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\4b&a\end{pmatrix} = aI+bJ$ ($J^2=4I$). Subring = contains $0,1$, closed under $-$ and $\cdot$; commutative iff the product formula is symmetric.

title: §4.2 — Structure of algebras
body:
*Exam relevance: high — every ring/group exercise uses kernels, congruences and quotients.*

**Content:** **subalgebras** (4.26) and the criterion "closed under all operations" (4.27); images and preimages of submodels along morphisms are submodels (4.32); products (4.33); **congruences** on a $T$-algebra (4.34, 4.35); **quotient algebras** $M/\!\sim$ (4.39); the **kernel pair of a morphism is a congruence** (4.42) and every congruence is the kernel of its projection; congruences form a complete lattice (4.48); **free** $T$**-algebras** and term algebras (4.49–4.51).

**Rings: ideals ↔ congruences.** For a congruence, $\mathfrak{a} = [0]$ is an ideal; conversely $a \sim b \iff a - b \in \mathfrak{a}$.

**Exam recipes:**
- **Ideal ⇒ exhibit it as a kernel** of a ring morphism ($A \mapsto a$, $A \mapsto d$, $aI+bJ \mapsto a+2b$). Then the first isomorphism theorem gives $R/\mathfrak{a} \cong \mathrm{im}$ — "$R/\mathfrak{a}$ is a field", "$R/\mathfrak{a} \simeq k$".
- **Not an ideal** of a bigger ring: one product that leaves $\mathfrak{a}$.
- Direct image of an ideal is an ideal **if** the morphism is surjective (inclusion of a subring = counterexample).
- Map between quotients $[A]_{\mathfrak{b}} \mapsto [A]_{\mathfrak{a}}$: well defined iff $\mathfrak{b} \subseteq \mathfrak{a}$; kernel $\mathfrak{a}/\mathfrak{b}$.
- **Normal subgroup:** closed under conjugation, or the preimage of a normal subgroup under a morphism.
- **Restricting a congruence** $U$ on $R$ to a submodel $S$: $V = U \cap S^2 = \ker(ip)$ is a congruence and $S/V \hookrightarrow R/U$ (Sept 2023 ex. 3).
